title: As yourself

cards: Leviticus can look like the hard book: offerings, skin diseases, rules for a plague in the walls of a house. Some readers who set out to read the Bible straight through stall right there.
But chapter nineteen, in among rules about harvests and wages and fabrics, holds a line some people know by heart without knowing where it comes from.
It sits in the middle of a verse, and the first half of that verse changes how it sounds.

teach.b: First, the whole verse. The King James text reads: "Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD."
It lands right after revenge and grudges: here, loving the neighbor starts with putting a grudge down.

Around the verse are very practical laws: leave the corners of your field and the fallen grapes for the poor and the stranger; don't keep a worker's wages overnight; don't put a stumbling block before the blind.

Third, the great principle. Jewish tradition records Rabbi Akiva calling this verse a great principle of the Torah. And the Talmud tells of a man who asked Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stood on one foot.
Hillel answered: what is hateful to you, don't do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn.
Jesus quotes the same verse in the Gospels, a Jewish teacher quoting the Torah.
And the two words at the end quietly assume something: that people want good things for themselves, and that the neighbor's wants are just as real.

how: Jews read Leviticus 19 in the Torah cycle as part of the portion called Kedoshim, and Hillel's answer to the man on one foot is taught in Jewish schools and sermons; Christians know the verse through Jesus' quotation of it in the Gospels.

games.why: Hillel gives him one line, calls the rest commentary, and sends him off to learn.

practice: Bring one neighbor to mind: the person next door, down the hall, at the next desk, someone you see often and rarely speak to. Breathing in, remember that they want an ordinary good day, just as you do.
Breathing out, if you're holding a small grudge against them, see whether you can set it down for now.

wordCard.voice: As yourself. From Leviticus nineteen: love thy neighbor as thyself, set right after a ban on grudges, in a chapter of laws that feed the poor. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: and you shall love your neighbor as yourself, Leviticus 19:18.

carryVoice: Your line: love has hands. It starts with a grudge set down. Back tomorrow, with the stranger.
